rv.q: The Comeuppance completes Jacobs-Jenkins’ residency at Signature and is his third masterpiece there.
Combining and advancing them, “The Comeuppance” is a richer and fully mature work.
Here’s a drama where Branden Jacobs-Jenkins both sums up and reconfigures the present moment.
Eric Ting, the director, has choreographed their intimacies intricately, and with loving attention to the unspoken histories behind their interactions.
Director Eric Ting deftly guides a superb cast, all of whom make the most of their carefully calibrated roles.
A canny cocktail of dark comedy and social observation, The Comeuppance is the most assured work yet from Jacobs-Jenkins, a writer who finds a fresh approach with each new play.
Eberhardt exudes charisma, and despite all of Emilio’s scab-picking, he grabs not only our attention but our sympathy.
We may think they’re behaving badly, that they’re living shitty lives, or that they’re doing the best they can–but that deserved penalty awaits anyway.

This play is an experience and reminder of those years upon years you spent around the same people, and you leave—finally, phew—wanting to return different, break from the mold, feel like you’ve done something extraordinary.
At least it presents its questions in a visually interesting, genre-bending manner, with a reminder that Death becomes all of us.
The play should leave the audience with a good deal to think about and talk over.
A playwright brilliant enough to make us think about life and death in a new way should probably be excused for making us wait to pee.
It’s creepyuntil Death disappointingly demystifies itself by talking too much.
Despite the two-hour and fifteen-minute play, without an intermission, my butt never twitched once. My focus never drifted once.
Director Eric Ting keeps the 2¼-hour play moving smoothly, modulating the confrontations and quieter moments so well that one scarcely notices there's no intermission.

cn.t: Critics praise Branden Jacobs-Jenkins's sharp, timely play about former classmates reuniting, with Death as a character. Eric Ting's expert direction and the innovative portrayal of mortality elevate this compelling examination of millennial life.
